title: Spring Lecture #40: Testing Spring Boot Applications | JUnit 5, Mockito & MockMvc
sources: code/springTestingDemo (PriceCalculator, ProductService, ProductController, PriceCalculatorTest, ProductServiceTest, ProductControllerTest, ProductRepositoryTest)
topics: Unit vs slice vs integration tests

questions.question: `PriceCalculatorTest` has a `@BeforeEach void setup()` that creates `new PriceCalculator()` and two `@Test` methods. How many times does `setup()` run when the class's tests are executed?
options: Once, before the first test, and the same instance is shared
Twice: once before each test method, so every test starts from a fresh, predictable state
Three times: once for the class and once per test
Zero times unless the class is annotated with `@SpringBootTest`
questions.explanation: `@BeforeEach` runs before every test method, giving each test a predictable starting state; with two tests it runs twice. Running once before all tests is what `@BeforeAll` is for. JUnit processes these annotations itself, without any Spring context.

questions.topic: Unit vs slice vs integration tests
questions.question: A teammate adds `@SpringBootTest` and `@Autowired PriceCalculator` to `PriceCalculatorTest` "so the calculator is a real Spring bean". The suite becomes noticeably slower. What does the lecture recommend?
options: Keep it: every class annotated with `@Service` must be tested through the Spring context
Replace it with `@WebMvcTest`, which is faster than `@SpringBootTest`
Mock `PriceCalculator` with `@MockitoBean` so the context starts faster
Remove the Spring annotations and create it with `new PriceCalculator()` in a plain JUnit test, because it has no dependencies and its logic can be tested directly
questions.explanation: The core principle is to use the smallest environment that can prove the behaviour. `PriceCalculator` is plain Java logic, so a plain JUnit test (as in the lecture code) is fastest and isolates the calculation. Mocking the class under test would test nothing, and `@WebMvcTest` is for the web layer.
questions.source: notes p5-7, p10-11 (unit tests, testing pyramid, first JUnit test), p38 (core principle)

questions.question: Using the lecture's `PriceCalculator` below, what is the outcome of this test?
options: It passes, because both inputs are invalid and an `IllegalArgumentException` is thrown
It fails at `assertThrows`, because two exceptions are thrown
It fails at `assertEquals`: the price check runs first, so the message is "price cannot be negative"
It errors, because `assertThrows` cannot be combined with `assertEquals`
questions.explanation: The method throws on the first failing check, which is `price < 0`, so only one exception with "price cannot be negative" is thrown. `assertThrows` succeeds (the type matches) and returns that exception, and the message assertion then fails. Testing one behaviour per test (separate negative-price and discount-above-100 tests) avoids this confusion.

questions.question: Why does `ProductServiceTest` use `@Mock` for the repository while `ProductControllerTest` uses `@MockitoBean` for the service?
options: There is no Spring context in the service test, so Mockito creates a plain mock field; in `@WebMvcTest` Spring creates the controller, so the mock must be a bean in the test `ApplicationContext`, which `@MockitoBean` provides
`@Mock` only works for interfaces and `@MockitoBean` only works for classes
`@MockitoBean` creates a real bean wrapped in a spy, while `@Mock` creates a fake
They are interchangeable; the choice is a matter of style
questions.explanation: In the service test, `MockitoExtension` creates the `@Mock` and `@InjectMocks` passes it to the `ProductService` constructor, with no Spring involved. In a `@WebMvcTest`, Spring builds `ProductController`, and its constructor needs a `ProductService` bean; `@MockitoBean` adds or replaces that bean with a Mockito mock. A plain `@Mock` field would never reach the Spring context.
questions.source: notes p17-19, p29-30 (@Mock, @InjectMocks, @Mock vs @MockitoBean); code: ProductServiceTest, ProductControllerTest

questions.question: A teammate copies the lecture's `ProductServiceTest` but forgets `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`. What happens when this test runs?
options: It passes, because JUnit Jupiter processes `@Mock` and `@InjectMocks` by itself
It fails with a `NullPointerException` at the `when(...)` line: without the extension the annotated fields are never initialized, so `productRepository` is null
It fails because `ProductService` is created without its repository and `getProductById` returns null
It starts a Spring context and uses the real `ProductRepository`
questions.explanation: JUnit knows how to run tests but does not process Mockito annotations; `MockitoExtension` is what initializes `@Mock` and `@InjectMocks` fields. Without it both fields stay null, so `productRepository.findById(1L)` inside `when(...)` throws a `NullPointerException` before the service is even called. No Spring context is involved in this test.
questions.source: notes p17-19 (Configuring Mockito with JUnit); code: ProductServiceTest

questions.question: The notes' project has Spring Security on the classpath. A `@WebMvcTest` for `POST /api/products` is annotated with `@WithMockUser` and sends valid JSON, but the response is 403 instead of 201. What is the most likely fix?
options: Replace `@WithMockUser` with `@SpringBootTest`, because security only works with the full context
Add `@MockitoBean` for the `SecurityFilterChain`
Change the expected status to 403, since mock users can never create data
Add `.with(csrf())` to the request: the security filters run in MockMvc, and CSRF protection rejects unsafe methods without a token
questions.explanation: `@WebMvcTest` loads the security filters, so MockMvc requests pass through them. `@WithMockUser` handles authentication (otherwise the result would be 401), but POST, PUT and DELETE still need a CSRF token when CSRF protection is enabled, which `.with(csrf())` supplies. Mocking the filter chain or using the full context does not remove CSRF.
questions.source: notes p28-29, p33-36 (@WebMvcTest loads security filters, POST test, handling Spring Security)

questions.question: This variant of the lecture's `shouldCreateProductWhenNameIsUnique` runs with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`. `Product` has only Lombok `@Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor @AllArgsConstructor` (no `equals`). Why does the test fail?
options: The `save` stub was registered for a different `Product` instance; Mockito matches arguments with `equals`, which here is identity, so `save(request)` doesn't match the stub (strict stubs report the argument mismatch; without a match `save` would return null)
`existsByName` returns `true` by default for unstubbed calls, so the service throws
`assertEquals(10L, ...)` always fails because `getId()` returns a `Long`
The test passes; Mockito compares objects field by field
questions.explanation: Without a matcher, Mockito compares stubbed arguments using `equals`. `Product` doesn't override it, so a new object with the same fields is not equal to `request`. The lecture's version stubs `save(request)` with the same instance; alternatively `any(Product.class)` would work. An unstubbed `boolean` method returns `false`, so `existsByName` is not the problem.
questions.source: code: ProductServiceTest, Product; notes p22-26 (product creation tests, argument matchers)

questions.question: A developer adds `Optional<Product> findByNameIgnoreCase(String name)` and 'tests' it by mocking the repository and stubbing `findByNameIgnoreCase("laptop")` to return a product. The test is green, but the query fails in production because of a typo in the property name. What should have been done?
options: Also verify the mock with `verify(repository).findByNameIgnoreCase("laptop")`
Use `@WebMvcTest`, which runs repository queries through MockMvc
Test the real repository in a `@DataJpaTest` slice with an embedded database such as H2, so Spring Data and Hibernate actually create and execute the query
Use `@MockitoBean` instead of `@Mock` so the stub goes through Spring Data
questions.explanation: A mocked repository only returns what the test configured, so it proves nothing about the real query or mapping. `@DataJpaTest` loads entities, Spring Data repositories, Hibernate and an embedded database, and each test runs in a transaction that is rolled back. `verify` only checks the call, and `@MockitoBean` is still a mock.
questions.source: notes p36-38 (Why repository tests use a database, @DataJpaTest, H2); code: ProductRepositoryTest

questions.topic: Unit vs slice vs integration tests
questions.question: Following 'use the smallest test environment that can prove the behaviour', which mapping fits these three checks? (1) the discount-above-100 rule in `PriceCalculator`; (2) `POST /api/product` returns 201 with the saved product as JSON; (3) the derived query `existsByName` works against the real schema.
options: (1) `@SpringBootTest`; (2) `@DataJpaTest`; (3) Mockito `@Mock` repository
(1) plain JUnit; (2) `@WebMvcTest` + MockMvc with a `@MockitoBean` service; (3) `@DataJpaTest` with an embedded database
(1) `@WebMvcTest`; (2) plain JUnit calling `controller.createProduct(...)` directly; (3) `@SpringBootTest` against MySQL
(1) Mockito `@InjectMocks`; (2) `@SpringBootTest` with Postman; (3) `@WebMvcTest`
questions.explanation: Plain logic needs only JUnit; the HTTP contract (mapping, JSON conversion, status code) needs Spring MVC's infrastructure via `@WebMvcTest` and MockMvc, with the service mocked; a repository query needs a real JPA slice and database. Calling the controller method directly would skip mapping, JSON and status handling, and mocking the repository can't validate a query.
questions.source: notes p26-28 (why not call the controller directly), p37-38 (quick comparison, core principle)

questions.question: In the lecture's `ProductControllerTest`, a teammate deletes the `@MockitoBean private ProductService productService;` field because the GET test 'doesn't really need a service'. What happens when the test class runs?
options: The test context fails to load: `@WebMvcTest` scans controllers but not `@Service` beans, so no `ProductService` bean exists for `ProductController`'s constructor
Spring automatically creates the real `ProductService`, which then fails because no database is configured
The test runs and the controller receives `null` for `productService`, causing a 500 response
MockMvc skips the controller and returns 404
questions.explanation: `@WebMvcTest` is a slice: it loads controllers, MVC infrastructure, JSON conversion and filters, but regular `@Component`/`@Service` beans are not scanned. `ProductController` requires a `ProductService` in its constructor, so the context cannot be built and the tests error out before any request is made. `@MockitoBean` supplies that missing bean as a mock.
questions.source: notes p28-30 (@WebMvcTest, @Mock vs @MockitoBean); code: ProductControllerTest, ProductController
